messages.subject: Reproducibility of an SPDE model in R-INLA
parts:
Dear INLA community, 

I am fitting an SPDE-occupancy model in R-INLA, with the spatial field grouped by year-month using an iid group structure. I set num.threads = 1.

However, when I run exactly the same model using the same dataset and the same script, I obtain different results across runs. In some cases, the WAIC differs by more than 50.

I am using WAIC for model selection, so this level of run-to-run variation is critical for my analysis.

Is it expected that R-INLA can produce different results when the same dataset, model specification, and script are used repeatedly? If not, what settings or diagnostics would you recommend to ensure reproducibility?

Thank you in advance for your advice.


<Script>

## Spatial field index and projector matrix
st_index <- INLA::inla.spde.make.index(
  name = "spatial.field",
  n.spde = spde$n.spde,
  n.group = 12
)

A_matrix <- INLA::inla.spde.make.A(
  mesh = mesh,
  loc = coords_sp,
  group = spatial.field.group,
  n.group = 12
)

## Effects used in the model
occ_effects <- data.frame(
  Intercept = 1,
  var = inla_dat$var,
  year = inla_dat$year
)

## INLA stack
stack <- INLA::inla.stack(
  data = list(
    dummy = rep(NA_real_, nrow(inla_dat))
  ),
  responses = list(
    YX = YX
  ),
  A = list(
    A_matrix,
    1
  ),
  effects = list(
    spatial.field = st_index,
    occ_effects
  )
)

## Model
formula_st <- YX ~ -1 +
  Intercept +
  var +
  f(year, model = "iid") +
  f(
    spatial.field,
    model = spde,
    group = spatial.field.group,
    control.group = list(model = "iid")
  )

## INLA fitting
fit <- INLA::inla(
  formula_st,
  data = INLA::inla.stack.data(stack),
  family = "occupancy",

  control.fixed = list(
    prec = 1 / 2.72,
    prec.intercept = 1 / 2.72
  ),

  control.predictor = list(
    A = INLA::inla.stack.A(stack),
    compute = FALSE
  ),

  control.compute = list(
    openmp.strategy = "default",
    dic = FALSE,
    waic = TRUE,
    cpo = FALSE,
    config = FALSE,
    mlik = FALSE
  ),

  control.family = ctrl_family,

  num.threads = 1,

  verbose = FALSE
)

Hi,

you're using old syntax with inla.spde.make.* and inla.stack(), making it difficult to follow.
Can you try the below that specifies the same model using the inlabru interface?
Also, please provide the summary(fit) output, as often, numerical instability is due to non-identifiability of some parameters, which may be clear from the summary output.
It looks from the code below that the Intercept and year components are mutually non-identifiable, for example, although the shrinkage effect in the "iid" model normally manages to overcome that.
However, since the spatial model is _also_ iid across year, this might still be the problem. But look at and show the summary() output to (perhaps) find out...
Finn

library(inlabru)
## Model
formula_st <- YX ~ 0 + # Or better, a direct inla.mdata(Y,X) call, where Y and X are in the inla_dat object, or constructible from it
  Intercept(1, prec.linear = 1/2.72) +
  var(var, prec.linear = 1/2.72) +
  year(year, model = "iid") +
  spatial(
    geometry, # assuming 'sf' data storage in inla_dat. Raw coordinates like "coord_sp" are strongly discouraged as it loses CRS information.
    model = spde,
    group = year,
    ngroup = 12

control.group = list(model = "iid")
  )

# Note: group model "iid" is arguably better done as replicate = year instead of group.

fit <- bru(
  formula_st,
  data = inla_dat,
  family = "occupancy",
  control.family = ctrl_family,
  options = list(

control.compute = list(
      openmp.strategy = "default",
      dic = FALSE,
      waic = TRUE,
      cpo = FALSE,
      config = FALSE,
      mlik = FALSE
    ),

num.threads = "1:1:1",
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)

I also reconsidered the model structure in light of your comment. In my original model, I included an iid year effect together with spatial fields grouped by month, with an iid group model. Since monthly meteorological variables are also included among the candidate covariates(tmp, wind), I was concerned that the month-specific spatial effects might compete with these covariates in explaining monthly spatial variation.

I therefore also fitted the model after removing the month-specific iid grouping of the spatial effect and ran this modified model three times using the same dataset. I would guess that an additional rerun would be benefitial here; see ?inla.rerun
?bru_rerun

by default 'inla.rerun' will run with tigther tolerances, by scaling the ones
used in the previous run.

its a misconseption that, because inla is deterministic then it has to produce
the same results after each run. the main source of 'randomness' is in the
parallel computing, which is impossible to control unless turning it off
completely. also, non-gaussian likelihoods, makes it worse because of the inner
optimisation whos initial values depends on the parellisation, ie the prevous
function evaluation in the same thread. its possible to set options to make it
produce the same results every time, but it has to run serial, and some internal
optimisations turned off.

be aware that WAIC (and similarly, DIC) is a _sum_, and not a _mean_, meaning
that the WAIC estimate computed has (numerical) 'variance' that scales with
'n'=number of observations. if 'n' is high, then you're looking at an 'numerical
error' of order \sqrt{n}. so the 'error' might look high, but its not, really.

I would try to add

fit <- bru(...)
fit <- bru_rerun(fit)

as the second call is much quicker than the first call. similar with inla

r <- inla(...)
r <- inla.rerun(r)

this generally improves stability if the model is very sensitive

Best
H

Dear  Håvard  ,

Thank you very much for this very helpful information. I learned a lot from your explanation that deterministic computation does not necessarily mean that exactly the same numerical results will be obtained in every run.

Following your suggestion, I applied bru_rerun() to the repeated fits. The WAIC values still showed noticeable variation, and the estimated hyperparameter for the iid year effect also remained unstable even after rerunning the models.

I therefore reconsidered the treatment of year in the model. Since my dataset covers only four years, I wondered whether estimating year as an iid random effect might be difficult in this setting. I modified the model so that year was instead included as a categorical fixed effect. After applying bru_rerun(), the WAIC values from three repeated runs differed by less than 0.1, and the estimated year effects were also highly consistent among the runs.

Based on these results, I suspect that treating year as an iid random effect may have been one of the main sources of the numerical instability in this model. Does this interpretation seem reasonable to you?

I also wanted to mention the size of the dataset, since you pointed out that the numerical variation in WAIC depends on the number of observations. The dataset contains approximately 77,000 individual observations, corresponding to about 23,000 site-period units when repeated observations at the same site-period are grouped together.

I also have one question regarding the use of WAIC for model selection. With AIC, I had generally interpreted models within 2 AIC units of the minimum as having similarly strong support. In this analysis, I was planning to use a similar criterion for WAIC: to retain models with ΔWAIC < 2 as a set of well-supported models and then construct a predictive ensemble using CPO-based stacking.

However, your explanation about the numerical variability of WAIC made me wonder whether using a fixed cutoff such as ΔWAIC = 2 is appropriate, particularly when WAIC values can vary between repeated runs of exactly the same model and dataset. It also seems that such numerical variation could affect both the identification of the minimum-WAIC model and the selection of models considered equivalent to it.

In this situation, would you recommend another way to identify a set of well-supported candidate models before stacking? I would greatly appreciate your advice on an appropriate criterion for model screening when numerical variation in WAIC is not negligible.

Best regards,


2026年10月14日水曜日 13:22:59 UTC+9 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue):

I would guess that an additional rerun would be benefitial here; see ?inla.rerun
?bru_rerun

by default 'inla.rerun' will run with tigther tolerances, by scaling the ones
used in the previous run.

its a misconseption that, because inla is deterministic then it has to produce
the same results after each run. the main source of 'randomness' is in the
parallel computing, which is impossible to control unless turning it off
completely. also, non-gaussian likelihoods, makes it worse because of the inner
optimisation whos initial values depends on the parellisation, ie the prevous
function evaluation in the same thread. its possible to set options to make it
produce the same results every time, but it has to run serial, and some internal
optimisations turned off.

be aware that WAIC (and similarly, DIC) is a _sum_, and not a _mean_, meaning
that the WAIC estimate computed has (numerical) 'variance' that scales with
'n'=number of observations. if 'n' is high, then you're looking at an 'numerical
error' of order \sqrt{n}. so the 'error' might look high, but its not, really.

I would try to add

fit <- bru(...)
fit <- bru_rerun(fit)

as the second call is much quicker than the first call. similar with inla

r <- inla(...)
r <- inla.rerun(r)

this generally improves stability if the model is very sensitive

Best
H

parts: On Wed, 2026-10-14 at 01:53 -0700, Emi Yamaguchi wrote:

> I also have one question regarding the use of WAIC for model selection. With
> AIC, I had generally interpreted models within 2 AIC units of the minimum as
> having similarly strong support. In this analysis, I was planning to use a
> similar criterion for WAIC: to retain models with ΔWAIC < 2 as a set of well-
> supported models and then construct a predictive ensemble using CPO-based
> stacking.
> However, your explanation about the numerical variability of WAIC made me
> wonder whether using a fixed cutoff such as ΔWAIC = 2 is appropriate,
> particularly when WAIC values can vary between repeated runs of exactly the
> same model and dataset. It also seems that such numerical variation could
> affect both the identification of the minimum-WAIC model and the selection of
> models considered equivalent to it.
> In this situation, would you recommend another way to identify a set of well-
> supported candidate models before stacking? I would greatly appreciate your
> advice on an appropriate criterion for model screening when numerical
> variation in WAIC is not negligible.

'theory' says essentially what you say, whether you use 2 or 5 or something
along those lines.

reality says something different, as WAIC is a sum

WAIC = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i

and each w_i has to be computed, then (as we discussed), the 'numerical error'
in WAIC will scale like \sqrt{n}, we hope.

this means if 'n' is large, then the accuracy of each w_i needs to be
o(1/\sqrt{n}) for 'error in WAIC' to be o(1). if you think the INLA(-BRU)
results are bad, let us recall that most use of WAIC estimates are using MCMC.
then you can do the math...

Best
H

Dear  Håvard,

Thank you very much for your valuable comments. Your explanation about the numerical error in WAIC, particularly how it can increase with sample size, was very helpful.  
Based on your comments, I am now reconsidering my current model-selection criterion of ΔWAIC < 2. I think the criterion should be interpreted more cautiously, taking into account the numerical variability of WAIC in a large dataset rather than treating the cutoff as an absolute threshold.  
Again, I really appreciate all your help. I have learned a great deal from your explanations.  

Best regards,


Emi Yamaguchi
